content: The inclusion of daily micronutrient powders (MNPs) in dietary patterns resulted in the absence of whole grains and legumes, which are significant sources of magnesium. This created a nutritional gap. Further refinements to dietary models could potentially address this gap while still meeting target nutrient requirements. However, the inclusion of small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) daily reduced the iron gap but did not eliminate it, achieving 59% of the nutrient reference value (NRV) compared to 28% in the best-case scenario. Like MNPs, the SQ-LNS scenario also showed a magnesium gap and additional gaps for potassium (76% of NRV) and choline (82% of NRV). Moreover, this scenario exceeded the upper limit (UL) for zinc intake. Further iterations would be necessary to balance nutrient gaps and excesses, but achieving this might be challenging without completely removing staple foods, as SQ-LNS displaced other complementary foods. Daily servings of Super Cereal Plus increased the iron gap and introduced significant new gaps for several minerals, thiamin, and choline. This was due to the displacement of other nutrient-rich foods. Models incorporating fortified items provided insights into whether lower-quality, less expensive food patterns could meet nutritional needs if fortified items were included. When MNPs were given daily, the food pattern included minimal starchy staples (roots/tubers), a very small amount of egg (less than one per week), a variety of vegetables, and a daily serving of 60 grams (one-quarter cup) of milk. Most nutrient needs could be met without flesh foods, but not without vegetables and dairy. Iterative modeling could address the magnesium gap. For SQ-LNS and Super Cereal Plus, food patterns were monotonous due to the displacement of other foods. These patterns consisted almost entirely of breast milk, the fortified item, and, in the case of SQ-LNS, the minimum required amount of staple foods. These patterns did not meet all target nutrient needs and were unlikely to do so without reducing the proportion of breast milk and increasing the inclusion of other complementary foods. For infants aged 9 months, modifying food patterns by eliminating food groups, restricting staples to one type, increasing staple quantities, or introducing unhealthy items had minimal impact on nutrient gaps. Iron gaps slightly increased in many scenarios, but no new gaps were introduced except for a small fat gap when staple foods were increased to 21 servings per week. Except for iron and vitamin D, many food patterns could meet nutrient needs for this age group as long as a diversity of whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and protein foods were included. Including one unhealthy item per day did not create nutrient gaps. However, scenarios with multiple unhealthy items were not modeled. For younger infants, the inclusion of any fortified items eliminated the carbohydrate gap and substantially reduced the vitamin D gap. However, vitamin D levels remained at only 43-54% of the NRV when fortified items were consumed daily. Other impacts varied by product. For 9-month-old infants, only MNPs could close iron gaps and meet target nutrient needs with minimal protein foods. However, meeting all targets required a small amount of dairy and ample fruits and vegetables. Since other fortified items did not close the iron gap, food patterns with daily SQ-LNS or Super Cereal Plus remained diverse, including a variety of vegetables and protein subgroups, but lacked dairy and included little or no fruit. For 9-month-old infants, feasible best-case patterns had no gaps for target nutrients. Scenarios that eliminated food groups introduced new nutrient gaps. For example, scenarios without vegetables or animal-source protein foods introduced iron gaps (88-94% of NRV). The scenario without animal-source protein foods introduced a small gap for vitamin B12 (95% of NRV), and the scenario without fruits or vegetables introduced a small gap for fiber (96% of NRV). Scenarios with monotonous staple foods or increased quantities of staples did not introduce new nutrient gaps as long as a diversity of fruits, vegetables, and protein foods were included. Scenarios with no whole grains or only roots/tubers/plantains slightly exceeded the UL for copper. Including sweetened beverages seven days a week introduced a small gap for thiamin but no other new gaps, provided a diversity of whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and protein foods were included. Many modified scenarios for this group slightly exceeded the UL for copper. For 9-month-old infants, target nutrient needs could be met without fortified products. Scenarios with fortified products were somewhat less diverse, with fewer servings of whole grains and flesh foods and, except for MNPs, fewer servings of dairy. However, even scenarios with daily fortified products included three to five types of fruits and vegetables daily. Sensitivity analyses excluding flesh foods and assuming 5% iron absorption showed that daily MNPs eliminated the iron gap, while SQ-LNS reduced but did not eliminate it. Super Cereal Plus did not reduce the gap. For 9-month-old infants, feasible best-case patterns had gaps only for carbohydrate and vitamin D, with no gaps for target nutrients. Scenarios that eliminated food groups introduced new nutrient gaps. Scenarios without fruits or vegetables were low in vitamin C (81% of NRV) and had a small gap for the non-target nutrient linoleic acid (95%). Scenarios without flesh foods or animal-source protein foods were low in vitamin B12 (~92% of NRV). Restricting the variety of starchy staple foods did not introduce new nutrient gaps as long as a diversity of fruits, vegetables, and protein foods were included. Allowing one unhealthy item up to seven days a week also did not introduce new nutrient gaps. However, scenarios with multiple types of unhealthy items were not modeled. Many modified scenarios for this group slightly exceeded the UL for copper. In real-world food patterns approximated using population-level data from rural Bangladesh, rural southern Malawi, and Mexico, the percentage of energy from major food groups differed substantially from modeled best-case scenarios. The calculated nutrient content of these patterns fell short of target values for most nutrients in one or more settings. Nutrient targets were met in all cases only for protein, fatty acids, vitamins A and C, and niacin. In Bangladesh and Malawi, gaps were observed for choline and most B vitamins and minerals across all age groups. There were fewer gaps in Mexico, particularly for the oldest age group, but gaps remained for several B vitamins and minerals. As in the modeled scenarios, carbohydrate intake was low, and vitamin D intake was very low (0-9% of NRV) across all three settings. Fortified items provided only a partial solution to these gaps. All three fortified items filled gaps for some or all B vitamins. MNPs and SQ-LNS eliminated gaps for zinc and copper, and SQ-LNS reduced or eliminated the gap for calcium. However, gaps for choline, potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus remained in Bangladesh and Malawi for some age groups. Iron gaps were filled or reduced to the greatest extent by MNPs, followed by SQ-LNS, with Super Cereal Plus having a much smaller impact. However, particularly when assuming lower absorption, iron gaps remained and were very large in some scenarios. Overall, MNPs and SQ-LNS appeared to have more positive impacts than Super Cereal Plus, but nutrient gaps remained in all three settings.
